title: Mirkwood Bats and a doubled eminence trigger: one drain or two?

scenario.mana_available: {B}{B} untapped from two Swamps; three other lands untapped and unspent

stack.note: cast for its printed {B}{B}. Edgar Markov has NEVER been cast and is in the command zone; eminence applies from there.

scenario.question: Edgar Markov's eminence triggers on this cast and would create one 1/1 black Vampire token, which Anointed Procession replaces with two. Mirkwood Bats reads 'Whenever you create or sacrifice a token, each opponent loses 1 life' — singular 'a token'. (a) How many times does Mirkwood Bats trigger from this single doubled creation event: once, or once per token created? (b) Does the answer change if a second doubler (Mondrak, Glory Dominus) is present and four tokens are created at once? (c) Vampire Socialite's replacement effect is conditional on an opponent having lost life this turn; if the Mirkwood Bats trigger is the FIRST life loss of the turn, do the tokens that caused it enter with the +1/+1 counter?

extras.context: Assume no opponent has lost life this turn before this cast, and no other permanent has a relevant triggered or replacement ability. Vampire Socialite is on the battlefield solely to make part (c) askable; Gifted Aetherborn is a Vampire, so Socialite's 'each other Vampire you control enters' would reach both the tokens and the resolved creature if its condition is met. Anointed Procession is the only token doubler on the battlefield for parts (a) and (c); part (b) is hypothetical and should be answered from the rules rather than from this board.
extras.why_this_matters: Mirkwood Bats arrived with the deck's v1.0.0 paper list and is the only payoff in the 99 keyed on token CREATION rather than on a creature ENTERING. Stack 010 proved that three doublers turn one eminence trigger into eight tokens. Whether Bats reads that as one drain or eight is the difference between a rounding error and a win condition, and no artifact in this deck currently prices it either way.
extras.scope: One rules domain: triggered-ability event counting under a token-creation replacement effect, plus the conditional-replacement timing in (c). No combat, no state-based actions beyond those needed to finish the cast.

steps.action: You cast Gifted Aetherborn for {B}{B}. Edgar Markov's eminence ability — "Whenever you cast another Vampire spell, if Edgar is in the command zone or on the battlefield, create a 1/1 black Vampire creature token" — has an intervening 'if' clause; Edgar is in the command zone as you cast, so the ability triggers. Its own text states the zone it functions in, so it functions from the command zone with Edgar never having been on the battlefield (established by checker-passed stack 010, steps 1-2). It is put on the stack above the Gifted Aetherborn spell the next time a player would receive priority, all players pass, and it resolves first.
steps.effect: The eminence trigger begins to resolve. Gifted Aetherborn remains on the stack at pos 0. Both opponents are still at 40 and no opponent has lost life this turn.

citations.quote: When the trigger event occurs, the ability checks whether the stated condition is true. The ability triggers only if it is; otherwise it does nothing.
An ability that states which zones it functions in functions only from those zones.
Once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack as an object that’s not a card the next time a player would receive priority.
When all players pass in succession, the top (last-added) spell or ability on the stack resolves.

steps.action: The eminence trigger's instruction is to create one 1/1 black Vampire creature token. Anointed Procession is a permanent you control whose static ability generates a continuous replacement effect: "If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, it creates twice that many of those tokens instead." It is the only doubler on this board. The word 'instead' marks it a replacement effect, and the event it would replace — one token created under your control — is exactly what this resolving ability would do. Two preconditions are met rather than assumed. Edgar is still in the command zone as the trigger resolves, so the intervening 'if' holds a second time and the ability is not removed from the stack (603.4). And the Procession's precondition is that an EFFECT would create the tokens: CR 614.16 is written for that exact template and says these replacement effects apply when the effect of a resolving spell or ability creates a token, which a resolving triggered ability's token creation is.
steps.effect: The one-token creation never happens. The modified event happens instead: you create TWO 1/1 black Vampire creature tokens, in a single creation, and they are put onto the battlefield under your control as their owner.

citations.quote: Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects.
Static abilities create continuous effects, some of which are prevention effects or replacement effects.
If an event is replaced, it never happens. A modified event occurs instead, which may in turn trigger abilities.
To create one or more tokens with certain characteristics, put the specified number of tokens with the specified characteristics onto the battlefield.
The player who creates a token is its owner. The token enters the battlefield under that player’s control.
If the ability triggers, it checks the stated condition again as it resolves. If the condition isn’t true at that time, the ability is removed from the stack and does nothing.

Some replacement effects apply “if an effect would create one or more tokens” or “if an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent.” These replacement effects apply if the effect of a resolving spell or ability creates a token or puts a counter on a permanent

steps.action: ANSWER (c), first half: the two tokens do NOT enter with a +1/+1 counter. Vampire Socialite's second ability — "As long as an opponent lost life this turn, each other Vampire you control enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it" — is a static ability generating a replacement effect that modifies how those Vampires enter, so it is checked now, as the tokens are put onto the battlefield. A continuous effect from a static ability is not locked in: it applies at any given moment to whatever its text indicates, and its 'as long as' clause is false at this moment, because by the scenario's stipulation no opponent has lost life this turn. Mirkwood Bats has not even triggered yet (step 4), and a trigger does nothing when it triggers in any case.
steps.effect: Socialite's replacement effect is not applicable to this entry. The two 1/1 black Vampire tokens enter the battlefield with no counters on them: two 1/1s.

citations.quote: Continuous effects that read “[This permanent] enters . . .” or “[Objects] enter [the battlefield] . . .” are replacement effects.
To determine which replacement effects apply and how they apply, check the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield
A continuous effect generated by a static ability isn’t “locked in”; it applies at any given moment to whatever its text indicates.
Whenever a game event or game state matches a triggered ability’s trigger event, that ability automatically triggers. The ability doesn’t do anything at this point.

steps.action: ANSWER (a): Mirkwood Bats triggers TWICE — once per token created, not once per creation event. Its trigger event is written in the singular: "Whenever you create or sacrifice a token, each opponent loses 1 life." The event it is looking for is you creating A token, and creating a token is putting a token onto the battlefield; the single happening in step 2 put two tokens onto the battlefield, so it contains two occurrences of that event. One happening is treated as a single event by one ability and as multiple events by another, exactly as the CR's own blocked / blocked-by-a-creature example shows, and an ability triggers repeatedly when one event contains multiple occurrences — the CR's mass-land-destruction example triggers once per land within a single resolution. (Contrast the wording the doublers use: Anointed Procession and Mondrak both say 'one or more tokens', which describes the whole happening. Bats does not.)
steps.effect: Two Mirkwood Bats triggers have triggered. Nothing has happened yet — no life has been lost, and no opponent has lost life this turn as far as any other effect can see.

citations.quote: The text of triggered abilities and replacement effects defines the event they’re looking for. One “happening” may be treated as a single event by one ability and as multiple events by another.
this is one event for a triggered ability that reads “Whenever this creature becomes blocked” but two events for a triggered ability that reads “Whenever this creature becomes blocked by a creature.”
An ability triggers only once each time its trigger event occurs. However, it can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences.
the ability will trigger once for each land put into the graveyard during the spell’s resolution
To create a token is to put a token onto the battlefield.

steps.action: The eminence trigger finishes resolving and leaves the stack. Before any player receives priority, state-based actions are checked — no player is at 0 or less life, no creature has lethal damage or 0 toughness, so none are performed — and then the triggered abilities waiting to be put on the stack are put there. You control both Bats triggers and neither triggers on another ability triggering, so you put them on the stack in whichever order you choose, above the Gifted Aetherborn spell.
steps.effect: The stack, bottom to top: Gifted Aetherborn (pos 0), Mirkwood Bats trigger #1, Mirkwood Bats trigger #2. The two triggers are textually identical, so their order does not matter. You receive priority.

steps.effect: Opponent A 40 -> 39, Opponent B 40 -> 39. That is 1 life PER OPPONENT and 2 across this two-opponent pod — the two figures are not interchangeable. An opponent has now lost life this turn.

steps.effect: Opponent A 39 -> 38, Opponent B 39 -> 38. Total from the doubled eminence token: 2 life PER OPPONENT, 4 across this two-opponent pod. The Bats drain is exactly the number of tokens created, per opponent.

steps.action: ANSWER (c), second half: the counter arrives too late for the tokens and in time for the spell that caused them. The tokens are already on the battlefield; a replacement effect cannot go back in time and change an event that has already happened, and Socialite's ability is a replacement effect, not a triggered one, so there is nothing to look back and put counters on the tokens. But Socialite's continuous effect is not locked in: its condition is true from step 6 onward. All players pass, Gifted Aetherborn — a targetless creature spell — resolves and enters the battlefield, and it is another Vampire you control (Creature — Aetherborn Vampire, per cards.json), so the replacement effect now applies to ITS entry.
steps.effect: The two tokens remain 1/1s with no counters, permanently — nothing revisits them. Gifted Aetherborn enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it: a 3/4 with deathtouch and lifelink. Socialite's own "When this creature enters" trigger does not trigger; it refers to Socialite itself, which entered earlier. Nothing triggers Mirkwood Bats, which watches tokens, and Gifted Aetherborn is not a token.

citations.quote: Replacement effects must exist before the appropriate event occurs—they can’t “go back in time” and change something that’s already happened.
it applies at any given moment to whatever its text indicates
If the object that’s resolving has no targets, it becomes a permanent and enters the battlefield under the control of the spell’s controller.
To determine which replacement effects apply and how they apply, check the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield

steps.action: ANSWER (b), from the rules and not from this board: yes, the count scales, and it scales with the number of TOKENS in the final modified event — not with the number of doublers and not with the number of create instructions. With a second doubler (Mondrak, Glory Dominus) present, each replacement effect gets one opportunity to affect the event or any modified event that replaces it, so one token becomes two becomes four, and the modified event that actually happens is a single happening in which you create four tokens. The two doublers' different wordings are inert, and 614.16 is why: Anointed Procession's 'if an effect would create' applies not only to the resolving ability's own creation but also when another replacement effect has already replaced the event, so Procession is not left behind by Mondrak going first. Mirkwood Bats' singular trigger event then has four occurrences inside that one happening and triggers four times.
steps.effect: Four tokens created at once = four Mirkwood Bats triggers = 4 life lost PER OPPONENT (8 across a two-opponent pod, 12 across a three-opponent pod). Generally, N tokens created in one event = N triggers = N life per opponent. COUNTERFACTUAL, not a claim about a tracked board: checker-passed stack 010 proves the TOKEN COUNT only — its three doublers (Elspeth, Storm Slayer + Anointed Procession + Mondrak) turn one eminence trigger into eight tokens — and that board holds NO Mirkwood Bats, no Vampire Socialite, and its own passing final_state records both opponents at 40, 'unchanged; no damage dealt in this resolution'. Nobody lost life there and this resolution does not say they did. Add Mirkwood Bats to that board and the same eight tokens would be eight triggers: 8 per opponent, 16 across its two-opponent pod. Conversely this board (011) holds Bats but only one doubler, so it makes two tokens, not eight. The rules generalisation is established by step 4 alone and needs no sibling board.

citations.quote: A replacement effect doesn’t invoke itself repeatedly; it gets only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that may replace that event.
If an event is replaced, it never happens. A modified event occurs instead, which may in turn trigger abilities.
it can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences
The text of triggered abilities and replacement effects defines the event they’re looking for.
they also apply if another replacement or prevention effect does so, even if the original event being modified wasn’t itself an effect

steps.action: State-based actions are checked once more before any player next receives priority. No player is at 0 or less life (both opponents are at 38), no creature has lethal damage marked and none has 0 or less toughness. Nothing is performed and no ability is waiting to go on the stack.
steps.effect: The stack is empty and the board stands as recorded below.

citations.quote: Whenever a player would get priority (see rule 117, “Timing and Priority”), the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event.

final_state.summary: (a) Mirkwood Bats triggers ONCE PER TOKEN CREATED, not once per creation event: its trigger event is singular ('a token'), and the single doubled happening contains two occurrences of it (CR 700.1, 603.2c). Anointed Procession's doubled eminence token therefore drains 2 life per opponent — 4 across this two-opponent pod — not 1 and 2. (b) The count follows the number of tokens in the final modified event: two doublers and four tokens = four triggers = 4 per opponent. Doublers multiply the drain; the drain is not per doubler. Stated counterfactually, because no tracked board shows it: checker-passed stack 010 proves eight tokens from three doublers but holds no Mirkwood Bats and records both opponents at 40, so putting Bats on that board — a change to it — is what would make those eight tokens eight triggers. (c) NO — the tokens do not enter with Vampire Socialite's +1/+1 counter. Socialite's ability is a conditional replacement effect checked as each Vampire enters (614.1d, 614.12, 611.3a), and at that instant no opponent has lost life this turn: the Bats ability has only TRIGGERED, and a trigger does nothing until it is put on the stack and resolves (603.2, 603.3). The life loss arrives afterwards and cannot go back in time (614.4). The same delay works the other way for the spell that started it: by the time Gifted Aetherborn resolves, both Bats triggers have, so it enters as a 3/4 with the counter. The intuitive reading — 'the tokens caused the drain, so the drain should count for them' — is the wrong one.

Swamp x3 (two tapped for the {B}{B} that cast Gifted Aetherborn), Mountain, Plains

drain_arithmetic.note: Per-opponent and pod total are not interchangeable. Bats drains 1 per opponent per token created.

answers.a: Twice — once per token created. Two tokens from the doubled eminence trigger = 2 Bats triggers = 2 life per opponent.
answers.b: Yes, it scales: four tokens created at once = four triggers = 4 life per opponent. The count tracks tokens in the final modified event, not doublers. Any figure quoted for another board (e.g. stack 010's eight tokens) is counterfactual — 010 carries no Mirkwood Bats and its passing record has both opponents at 40.
answers.c: No. The tokens enter before the Bats trigger is even put on the stack, so Socialite's condition is false as they enter and cannot be applied retroactively. Gifted Aetherborn, resolving after both Bats triggers, DOES get the counter.

open_questions: This resolution prices one creation event. Whether Mirkwood Bats is a win condition in this deck depends on how many creation events the 99 generates per turn, which is a goldfish/engine question and not a rules one.

NEW IN ROUND 2, and it closes my round-1 step-null finding. Quote is verbatim from the second half of 603.4 ('If the ability triggers, it checks the stated condition again as it resolves. If the condition isn't true at that time, the ability is removed from the stack and does nothing'). Placement is correct: step 1 is the trigger triggering and going on the stack and quotes 603.4's first half; step 2 is its RESOLUTION, which is where the recheck belongs. The factual premise holds — the scenario stipulates Edgar has never been cast and is in the command zone, and nothing in steps 1-2 moves him — so the intervening 'if' is true a second time and the ability is not removed. Two quotes of one rule at two steps doing two different jobs is legitimate, not padding.

NEW IN ROUND 2; was my round-1 unsupported finding on this step. Quote verbatim from 614.16's opening. This is the FIRST clause and it does the first job: 614.16's own text names Anointed Procession's exact template in quotation marks ('if an effect would create one or more tokens'), which is word-for-word the card's precondition in cards.json, and then says these effects 'apply if the effect of a resolving spell or ability creates a token'. Edgar's eminence is a triggered ability and it is resolving, so its token creation is the effect of a resolving ability. The step's prose now NAMES the precondition and discharges it ('Two preconditions are met rather than assumed') instead of stepping over it. 609.1 is no longer needed as a second route — 614.16 says it in terms. Fully supported; no adjacency.

NEW IN ROUND 2; was my round-1 unsupported finding on this step. Judged INDEPENDENTLY of the step-2 use, because it is a different clause doing different work and it is the subtler of the two. Quote verbatim from 614.16's tail: 'they also apply if another replacement or prevention effect does so, even if the original event being modified wasn't itself an effect.' The claim is that a Mondrak-first ordering does not leave Anointed Procession behind — i.e. that Procession's 'if an EFFECT would create' precondition survives when the thing creating the tokens is Mondrak's replacement effect rather than a resolving ability. That is exactly what the quoted clause licenses, and the 'even if the original event being modified wasn't itself an effect' tail is permissive here rather than limiting, so unlike the 614.16 tail-clause trap in stack 010's earlier iteration it refutes no boundary this resolution asserts. I also checked the reverse ordering: Mondrak's wording carries no 'effect' precondition at all, so it applies either way — both orders give four, which is what makes the step's word 'inert' correct rather than convenient.
